title: Beef ragù
skill: A soffritto base, a long slow braise

notes.text: Sear the beef in three batches, and make sure your pot holds it all in about two layers with the sauce.

move.title: Sear, soffritto, then time
move.body: Ragù is the slow-cooked meat sauce of Italy. Today you'll sear big chunks of beef chuck until they're deep brown, build a soffritto of onion, carrot, and celery in the same pot, deglaze it, and add tomatoes. Then the lid goes on and the beef braises gently for hours, until it's soft enough to shred with a fork into the sauce.

callback.body: In adobo, you browned chicken thighs and braised them with the lid on until they were tender. Beef chuck is the same idea, but tougher, so it takes hours, not minutes. The steps you know just get more time.

why.title: Dry meat sears
why.body: A wet surface has to boil off its water before it can brown, and while it does, the meat steams. Patted dry, it starts browning the moment it hits the oil.

why.title: A deep brown crust
why.body: Searing isn't about cooking the meat through. It's about flavor: the brown crust, and the fond it leaves on the pot, flavor the whole sauce for hours. Leave each side alone until it lets go of the pot.

why.title: Soffritto
why.body: Onion, carrot, and celery chopped fine and cooked gently in oil are where many Italian sauces start. Chopped small, they melt into the sauce over the long cook, so you taste them without biting into them.

why.title: Cook the tomato paste
why.body: Tomato paste stirred into the hot pot for a couple of minutes turns from bright red to a darker rust color. That cooks off its raw, tinny taste and makes it sweeter and deeper.

why.title: Why chuck needs hours
why.body: Chuck is a hard-working shoulder muscle, full of tough connective tissue. A quick cook leaves it chewy. Hours of gentle heat melt that tissue into gelatin, which makes the meat fall apart and gives the sauce its rich, silky body.

why.title: A lazy bubble, not a boil
why.body: Boiling hard squeezes the meat fibers tight and dries them out, even under liquid. A gentle bubble, just a few breaking at a time, keeps the beef soft while the tough parts melt.

wrong.sign: The beef is gray, not brown
wrong.fix: The pot was crowded, or the meat was wet. Take some out, pat it dry, and sear in smaller batches until it's deep brown.

wrong.sign: The beef is still tough after the timer
wrong.fix: It needs more time, not more heat. Put the lid back on and check every 20 minutes.

wrong.sign: The sauce is sticking or scorching on the bottom
wrong.fix: Turn the heat down, stir in ½ cup of water, and don't scrape up anything black.

wrong.sign: The sauce is thin and watery
wrong.fix: After shredding, simmer it with the lid off, stirring now and then, until it's thick enough to cling to a spoon.

quiz.q: Why is the beef seared before it braises?
choices: The brown crust and fond flavor the whole sauce
quiz.explain: The long braise makes it tender; searing is for flavor.

quiz.q: Why does beef chuck need hours to cook?
choices: Its tough connective tissue needs time to melt
quiz.explain: The tissue melts into gelatin, and the meat falls apart.

quiz.q: What should the sauce look like while it braises?
quiz.explain: A hard boil dries out the meat, even under liquid.

substitutions.note: Gluten-free spaghetti turns soft quickly. Start tasting it 2 minutes before the box says.

steps.text: Pat the beef dry with paper towels. Cut it into chunks about 3 inches across, trimming off any thick pieces of hard white fat. Put the chunks on the plate, sprinkle the beef's salt and the pepper all over them, and turn them to coat every side.
steps.tip: Thin streaks of fat inside the meat stay. They melt in the long cook.

steps.text: Throw away the packaging and paper towels. Wash the knife and cutting board with hot, soapy water, and wash your hands with soap.
Dice the onion, carrot, and celery very small, about ⅛ inch, and put them together in the medium bowl. Peel and mince the garlic and keep it in the small bowl.
steps.look: Pieces smaller than a pea, all about the same size.

steps.text: Heat the oil in the large pot over medium-high heat until it shimmers.

With the tongs, lay half the beef in the pot with space between the chunks. Leave them alone until the bottoms are deep brown and let go of the pot, then turn them. Brown at least two sides, then move them back to the plate.
steps.look: A dark brown crust, and brown bits on the bottom of the pot.

steps.text: Sear the rest of the beef the same way and move it to the plate.
steps.tip: If the bottom of the pot is turning darker than dark brown, turn the heat down a little.

steps.text: Wash the tongs with hot, soapy water. They touched the raw beef.
Turn the heat down to medium-low. Add the soffritto and its salt. Cook, stirring and scraping the bottom of the pot now and then, until it's soft.
steps.look: Soft and shiny, the onion see-through. The water from the vegetables has loosened some of the brown bits.

steps.text: Add the garlic and tomato paste. Stir and cook until the paste turns a darker, rusty red.
Stand back and pour in the broth. Scrape the bottom of the pot hard with the wooden spoon until no brown bits are stuck to it.
steps.look: The bottom of the pot is clean.

steps.text: Add the crushed tomatoes, bay leaves, and oregano. Put the beef back in with any juices from the plate, and nestle it down into the sauce. Bring it to a bubble.
steps.tip: Pour the tomatoes slowly, close to the pot, so they don't splash.

steps.text: Turn the heat to low and put the lid on. Let it braise, stirring gently every 30 minutes and checking that it's still just barely bubbling.
steps.tip: Stay in the house while it braises. Set the timer for 30 minutes at a time if that helps you remember to stir.
steps.look: A few lazy bubbles at a time, not a boil.

steps.text: Lift out one chunk with the tongs and slide the thermometer into its middle. It needs to read at least 195°F, and fall apart when you press it with a fork. If it doesn't, put the lid back on and braise 20 minutes more.
steps.tip: Whole beef is safe at 145°F, but chuck isn't tender until about 195°F, when its tough tissue has melted.

steps.text: Fill the stockpot with the pasta's water at the sink, cover it, and set it over high heat to come to a boil.
steps.tip: Never carry a pot of boiling water.

steps.text: Turn off the heat under the ragù and take out the bay leaves. Pull the beef apart right in the pot with two forks, into bite-size shreds. Stir it through the sauce.
steps.look: No big chunks left, and the sauce is thick enough to cling to a spoon.

steps.text: When the water is boiling hard, add the pasta's salt and the spaghetti. Stir it with the tongs for the first 2 minutes, then boil it until it's tender with a little bite in the middle.
steps.tip: Check the box for its time, and taste a strand when the timer rings, after letting it cool.

steps.text: Set the colander in the sink. An adult pours the spaghetti into it, pouring away from both of you.
Taste the ragù and add a pinch more salt if it needs it. Serve it over the spaghetti, with parmesan on top if you like.

notes.text: Brown the beef in three batches, so it browns instead of steaming.

move.title: Brown, sweat, deglaze, simmer
move.body: Ragù bolognese is the meat sauce of Bologna, in Italy, made with ground beef and a soffritto of onion, carrot, and celery. Today you'll brown the beef, sweat the soffritto, deglaze the pot, and let it simmer for an hour and a half, until it's thick and rich enough to cling to every strand of spaghetti.

callback.body: In spaghetti marinara, you cooked an onion soft, then simmered tomatoes until a spoon left a path. Bolognese builds on that sauce: browned beef first, a finer vegetable base, and much more time.

sear.title: Brown it, don't steam it
sear.body: Ground beef browns only in a hot pot with room to spread out. Crowded, it lets out water and turns gray. Leave it alone between stirs, and the brown bits it leaves on the pot will flavor the whole sauce.

low-bubble.title: A lazy bubble, not a boil
low-bubble.body: A hard boil scorches the bottom and spatters the stove. A gentle bubble, just a few breaking at a time, lets the sauce thicken slowly without sticking.

add.title: Why simmer so long?
add.body: The beef is cooked through in minutes. The long simmer is for the sauce: the soffritto melts away, the flavors blend, and water cooks off until the sauce is thick and deep.

wrong.sign: The beef is gray, not brown
wrong.fix: The pot was crowded or not hot enough. Brown it in smaller batches, and leave it alone between stirs.
The heat was too high. Turn it down and add a spoonful of water. A little color is fine.

wrong.sign: The sauce is sticking or scorching on the bottom
wrong.fix: Turn the heat down, stir in ½ cup of water, and don't scrape up anything black.

wrong.sign: The sauce is thin and watery
wrong.fix: Simmer it with the lid off a little longer, stirring now and then, until it's thick enough to cling to a spoon.

quiz.q: What's the difference between browning the beef and sweating the soffritto?
choices: Browning is hot and adds color; sweating is gentle and adds none

quiz.q: Why pour in broth and scrape the bottom of the pot?
choices: To lift the brown bits so their flavor goes into the sauce

quiz.q: What should the sauce look like while it simmers?
quiz.explain: A hard boil scorches the bottom.

add.text: Crumble half the beef into the pot in pieces, straight from the package, and spread it out.
Brown the rest of the beef the same way, with the rest of the beef's salt and pepper, and move it to the plate.
Push the beef on the plate into a pile and slide the thermometer into the middle. It needs to read at least 160°F. If it doesn't, put it back in the pot for a minute and check again.
Tip the pot a little and spoon all but about a tablespoon of the fat into the heatproof bowl. Let it cool, then throw it away in the trash, not down the sink.
add.tip: Leave the brown bits in the pot. They're the flavor.

heat.text: Heat the oil in the large pot over medium-high heat until it shimmers.

sear-1.text: Leave it alone for 2 minutes, then break it into crumbles with the wooden spoon. Sprinkle on half the beef's salt and pepper. Keep cooking, stirring only every minute or so, until it's browned with no pink left. Move it to the plate.
sear-1.look: Deep brown crumbles, and brown bits on the bottom of the pot.

wash-beef.text: Throw away the package and wash your hands with soap.

tomatoes.text: Add the crushed tomatoes, bay leaves, and oregano. Put the beef back in and stir. Bring it to a bubble.
tomatoes.tip: Pour the tomatoes slowly, close to the pot, so they don't splash.

braise.text: Turn the heat to low and set the lid on the pot slightly open, so steam can escape. Simmer, stirring every 15 minutes and checking that it's still just barely bubbling.
braise.tip: Stay in the house while it simmers. Set the timer for 15 minutes at a time if that helps you remember to stir.
braise.look: A few lazy bubbles at a time, not a boil.

water-on.text: About 30 minutes before the simmer is done, fill the stockpot with the pasta's water at the sink, cover it, and set it over high heat to come to a boil.
water-on.tip: Never carry a pot of boiling water.

serve.text: Turn off the heat under the ragù and take out the bay leaves. Taste it and add a pinch more salt if it needs it. Serve it over the spaghetti, with parmesan on top if you like.
serve.look: Thick enough to cling to a spoon.
